limits: Chapter 4 is a finite-alphabet IID typical-set/fixed-error lossy block-compression treatment, not a lossless coding theorem for general stationary sources.
Chapter 6 uses ideal real interval arithmetic and describes a basic LZ78-style dictionary parse; it does not supply finite-precision integer arithmetic guarantees.

The LZ theorem prose glosses ergodic as 'memoryless on sufficiently long timescales'; this is not a mathematical definition. The handoff replaces it with exact stationary/ergodic hypotheses from the complete Gray chapter and Stanford note.

The book's ideal arithmetic model and LZ discussion do not prove operational EOF, fixed-register overflow, or implementation termination details; these are supplemented by the complete Moffat-Neal-Witten paper and explicit local proof routes.

The article explicitly warns that bits_outstanding can grow without bound on some inputs; its own implementation may abort, periodically synchronize/reset, or use a wider counter. Fixed-register correctness therefore requires one of those policies.
The article's figures were inspected, but the companion implementation archive was not obtained.

proof_locators: §1.1 definitions and stationary-source expected length bound: PDF pp. 1-2.

limits: The note proves expected LZ78 entropy-rate universality for stationary finite-alphabet sources; it states but does not prove the individual-sequence finite-state theorem, whose complete primary proof is supplied by the separately read Ziv-Lempel 1978 article.

Its LZ77 phrase-length theorem assumes stationarity and ergodicity and refers to Wyner-Ziv 1989. The separately read Kontoyiannis 1998 article supplies a recurrence-time proof and exact match-length equivalence under finite-alphabet stationarity/ergodicity; the claim is limited to that match-length convention, not a full bit-level LZ77 code theorem.

The classical LZ78 and LZ77 results remain distinct: expected-rate LZ78 universality applies to stationary finite-alphabet sources, individual-sequence LZ78 is relative to finite-state information-lossless encoders, and the sliding-window LZ77 match-length limit is almost sure for finite-alphabet stationary ergodic sources.

proof_locators: Two-sided finite-alphabet process and recurrence/waiting definitions, internal pp. 1-2.
Theorem 1 and summability condition, internal p. 3; the theorem gives almost-sure upper recurrence and conditional-probability lower recurrence bounds.
Corollary 1 and conversion to the stationary-ergodic entropy limit, internal pp. 3-4.
Proof of Corollary 1 and Theorem 1 parts (i)-(ii), internal pp. 8-9.
Sliding-window match length L_m, exact recurrence equivalence, and stated inversion, internal p. 6.

limits: The recurrence/entropy theorem assumes a finite alphabet, a two-sided stationary ergodic law, and base-2 logarithms. It does not assert a countable-alphabet extension.

The source match definition allows candidate occurrences to overlap the current phrase when their starting shift is smaller than the phrase length; a strictly nonoverlapping window is a different operational convention.
The L_m/log m reciprocal formulation requires positive entropy. The all-entropy statement log m/L_m tending to h is valid with L_m=+infinity and log m/(+infinity)=0 when necessary.

In proof of Theorem 1(ii), the displayed harmonic-sum bound only needs at most one string per finite first-return distance; the printed phrase says exactly one. The local argument uses the weaker, sufficient at-most-one fact.
